paper_title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning engines over images, documents, webpages, and videos. However, many real-world visual tasks require information that the model cannot reliably infer from the input alone. Answering question may require localizing numerous tiny objects in dense scenes, retrieving external knowledge about long-tail entity, or computing quantities from intermediate measurements. Such tasks require additional multimodal evidence acquired through perception, search, and computation. Our inference-time scaling study (Fig. 1c) reveals diminishing returns at higher reasoning budgets: moving the base model from xhigh to max effort multiplies its model-token spending by 2.7 but improves its average score by only 0.7 points. This raises the question of whether further progress requires better access to task-relevant multimodal evidence, beyond additional reasoning over the initial input. Visual tool-use agents address this need by connecting MLLMs to perception models, search engines, and code execution (Hong et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2025a; Narayan et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b; Surıs et al., 2023; Gupta & Kembhavi, 2023). Building general harness around these tools presents two connected challenges. First, heterogeneous backends expose different calling conventions and return outputs such as segmentation masks, depth maps, and retrieved webpages that need to be presented in form the model can interpret. Second, subsequent reasoning steps may still need access to the underlying artifacts: rendered depth map supports visual inspection, but precise measurement requires its numerical values. Effective multimodal tool use therefore requires both consistent tool interfaces with evidence rendering and mechanism for retaining and reusing the resulting artifacts. We introduce OpenVLHarness, multimodal reasoning harness organized around capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering. Task-level interfaces define operations independently of particular backend, allowing tools to be replaced without changing the orchestrators task vocabulary. Evidence rendering converts heterogeneous outputs into observations that combine visualizations, concise descriptions, and compact structured information. For example, visual grounding accepts an image and textual query, then presents the detected regions through an annotated image and coordinates. Together, these mechanisms let the orchestrator invoke tools consistently and inspect their results in form suited to multimodal reasoning. Persistent multimodal memory makes the corresponding artifacts available across turns within query. Images, structured data, and web references are registered under reusable handles, allowing later calls to operate on earlier evidence. In the grounding example, the orchestrator can inspect the overlay, then reuse the retained masks and subsequently acquired depth array to measure depth within each region. Python Coding Agent supports such compositions: the orchestrator specifies computational objective in natural language, and code-generation session backed by the same backbone model writes program that executes over the stored data. The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. Together, they support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and computing over multimodal evidence. We evaluate OpenVLHarness on 22 benchmarks spanning grounded perception, visual search and deep research, general VQA and hallucination, and spatial reasoning, using eight open and proprietary MLLM backbones of different scales (Fig. 1a). Across these settings, OpenVLHarness consistently improves average performance over the base MLLMs by 9.712.6 percentage points and outperforms existing visual tool-use baselines (Fig. 1c). Scaling experiments on 22 benchmarks further show that OpenVLHarness also benefits from greater reasoning effort (Fig. 1c), suggesting that evidence acquisition and inference-time scaling are complementary. We conduct ablation studies to examine the incremental effects of the capability layer and memory, showing the value of both usable tool outputs and retained multimodal artifacts. Lastly, for users who would like to adapt our harness to custom domain, we further showcase two coding-agent-driven workflows for specialization: harness search edits prompts, tool descriptions, and output templates, while tool generation composes existing capabilities into new tools. Both operate without updating the underlying MLLM weights. Our contributions are: (1) capability layer that combines task-level tool interfaces with modelfacing evidence rendering for heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools; (2) persistent multimodal memory that retains addressable artifacts across turns and enables their reuse in sub-

sections.title: 2 HARNESS DESIGN
sections.content: OpenVLHarness augments an MLLM orchestrator with two complementary mechanisms (Figure 2). The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering, providing consistent access to tools and observations the orchestrator can inspect (Sec. 2.1). Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding artifacts and exposes them by reference for reuse across turns within query (Sec. 2.2). At each step, the orchestrator uses the observations and available memory references to select tool call or produce an answer. Python Coding Agent supports computation over stored artifacts, connecting outputs from different capabilities into multi-step procedures. The modular interfaces and renderers also support harness specialization through text edits and tool composition (Sec. 3.6).

sections.title: 2.1 CAPABILITY LAYER
sections.content: We design the capability layer with two goals: defining how the orchestrator invokes capability and rendering the resulting evidence for inspection. The first accommodates different backends behind consistent interface; the second addresses the heterogeneous formats of their outputs. Task-level tool interfaces. We define capability by the operation it provides, its typed inputs, and the evidence and reusable data it exposes. For example, visual grounding accepts an image reference and textual query and exposes object locations, associated metadata, and visualization; supporting backend may additionally provide segmentation masks. Each backend is wrapped to implement this task-level interface. Visual Grounding can thus use SAM 3 or Grounding DINO, and OCR can use PaddleOCR-VL or DeepSeek-OCR, while preserving the orchestrators calling convention (Appendix C). Backend selection can reflect accuracy, cost, and latency requirements. Our base instantiation includes nine capabilities: five for perceptionZoom-in, Visual Grounding,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: OCR, Depth Estimation, and Camera Trajectory; three for information seekingText Search, Image Search, and Webpage Visit; and Python Coding Agent for computation over intermediate results. Please refer to Appendix and Table 18 for their implementation details. Model-facing evidence rendering. Raw tool outputs often require additional processing to become useful observations. An RLE mask encodes region precisely, but serializing that encoding into the context does not show the orchestrator which object was segmented. Dense numerical arrays can likewise consume substantial context without providing useful, interpretable evidence. Each capability therefore includes an output processor that renders its result into model-facing observation. Depending on the capability, this observation combines visual attachments, concise natural-language descriptions, compact structured information, and references to reusable artifacts. Grounding can return labeled mask overlay with the number of detected objects and normalized bounding boxes; depth estimation can return colorized map; and Camera Trajectory can return visualization of the recovered trajectory. The underlying masks, arrays, and camera parameters are passed to memory for later reuse. Figure 2 illustrates grounding for cabinet in input image 3. The capability returns mask overlay with description of the five grounded objects and their bounding boxes, allowing the orchestrator to inspect the detections. If subsequent step requires depth measurement for each cabinet, this rendered observation supplies the visual context, while the retained masks and depth array supply the data for computation. The memory mechanism below connects these steps.

sections.title: 2.2 PERSISTENT MULTIMODAL MEMORY
sections.content: The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; persistent multimodal memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. later tool call must be able to identify particular image, mask, or array and access its contents. Repeating description of previous result does not provide this access. We maintain an explicit artifact registry for each query, with entries retained across its reasoning trajectory. The registry separates an artifacts payload from the handle used to reference it. The orchestrator sees available names and compact descriptors, while the harness retains the underlying values and resolves references when needed. The registry contains three categories: Image artifacts: input, tool-generated, and retrieved images, exposed through handles such as input image 3 and tool generated image 6. Duplicate images reuse an existing registry entry. Structured data bindings: named values containing boxes, scores, masks, depth arrays, camera parameters, OCR results, and other tool outputs. Each binding has descriptor identifying its fields and types, including array shapes where applicable. Web references: retrieved URLs exposed through handles such as webpage url 1, allowing later navigation without requiring the model to reproduce the original URL. Registering and reusing artifacts. After successful tool call, the harness registers supported artifacts and associates their handles with the capabilitys rendered observation. Images are delivered as visual attachments with named references; structured payloads remain accessible through data bindings. An Environment Update advertises the available image handles, data bindings, and web references after each tool turn, exposing the current namespace without repeating every artifacts full payload. In the cabinet example, the grounding call adds an overlay image and bindings for the detection data, including bounding boxes and RLE masks. When subsequent call refers to an artifact, the harness resolves its handle to the input required by the receiving tool. An image handle supplies the image for later visual operation, web reference supplies URL for Webpage Visit, and data binding supplies values for code execution. The orchestrator can thus reuse the grounding and depth results without reconstructing their contents from earlier descriptions. References connect retained evidence across tools and turns. The detailed representation and handles can be found in Appendix C.4 and Table 19.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 3: Qualitative examples of OpenVLHarness. (a) Camera poses, depth, and grounding are combined in code to measure 3D distance (Example 17). (b) Grounded crops are passed to OCR and image search, and the answer is verified on the web (Example 8). (c) Masks from two grounding queries are reconciled in code to reach the exact count (Example 1). Memory-grounded computation. To compute depth within the detected cabinets, the orchestrator delegates natural-language objective to the Python Coding Agent, such as compute the average depth within each detected region. The harness supplies descriptors of the available memory bindings to fresh code-generation context of the same backbone model. The generated program executes with the actual binding values available as named variables, allowing it to combine the grounding masks with the depth array. Execution results and feedback return in language, with supported output artifacts registered for subsequent reuse. The orchestrator can then use the result or revise the objective in later call. This mechanism also supports filtering detections, aggregating OCR values, and other computations over intermediate results without requiring the orchestrator to serialize large arrays into its request. The capability layer supplies reusable operations and interpretable observations; memory and code execution connect their outputs into longer reasoning procedures. Qualitative examples. Figure 3 shows three trajectories from our evaluation. In each, the agent chains several capabilities and reuses their outputs through memory: camera poses, depth maps, and grounding masks become bindings for exact 3D computation (a); grounded crops are passed by identifier to zoom-in, OCR, and image search before the answer is verified on the web (b); and masks from two grounding queries are reconciled in code to correct an undercount (c).

sections.title: 3.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: Across the evaluated backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average performance over the underlying base model and outperforms all existing training-free harnesses  (Table 1)  . On Qwen3-VL8B, it raises the 22-dataset average from 34.2 to 45.4 (+11.2), exceeding the strongest trainingfree baseline, OctoTools (31.8), by 13.6 points; on Qwen3-VL-32B, the average rises from 38.3 to 50.9 (+12.6). The gains extend to GPT-5 (44.4 55.7), GPT-6 Sol (52.7 64.3), and Kimi K3 (56.4 66.1) (Appendix Table 7). On the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, OpenVLHarness averages 33.45 across the 22 datasets, surpassing the training-based baselines AdaReasoner (25.29), PixelReasoner (28.02), and DeepEyesV2 (25.02), without updating model weights (Appendix Table 9). The GPT-6 results highlight that effective multimodal tool use depends on the harness. With GPT-6 Luna, Codex averages 43.8, below the no-tool baseline (45.8), while OpenVLHarness reaches 56.5. This comparison shows that coding-agent harness does not automatically improve multimodal reasoning. With GPT-6 Astra, OpenVLHarness improves all 22 benchmarks and raises the average from 60.3 to 70.2, the highest of any backbone. Grounded perception and visual search and deep research benefit substantially from dedicated vision experts and external retrieval, respectively. Gains on general VQA and hallucination and on spatial reasoning depend more on the backbone: Luna and Astra improve on every benchmark in these domains (Luna by less than one point on RealWorldQA, HallusionBench, and EmbSpatial), with average gains of +6.5/+7.5 on general VQA and hallucination and +6.5/+5.2 on spatial reasoning, respectively. This pattern is consistent with greater proficiency in using tools and reasoning over their visual evidence. The less consistent gains on Qwen3-VL-8B motivate the failure analysis and domain specialization in Secs. 3.5 and 3.6.

sections.title: 3.3 CAN MORE REASONING REPLACE THE HARNESS?
sections.content: OpenVLHarness makes several model calls per question, each carrying tool outputs and memory, so it spends more model tokens than prompting the base model directly. Figure 1c reports the 22-benchmark averages against model-token cost, and Table 2 breaks them down by domain. sections.title: 3.4 ABLATION STUDY
sections.content: Table 3 examines the two mechanisms introduced in Sec. 2: the capability layer, which combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering, followed by persistent multimodal memory, which makes the resulting artifacts addressable and reusable across turns. Starting from the no-tool baseline, we add raw tool access, then the capability layer, and finally memory, using textual-memory variant as an intermediate comparison (details in Appendix B.2). Raw tool access raises the overall average by +3.8 points at 8B and +4.3 at 32B, with the largest gains in grounded perception. Adding the capability layer restores full tool schemas and renders heterogeneous outputs into concise observations, yielding another +3.4 and +3.2 points. These gains support the joint value of task-level tool interfaces and model-facing evidence rendering; the comparison does not separate their individual contributions. Adding textual memory enables structured data bindings, web references, and Environment Updates, but represents tool-generated images only through descriptions, without reusable image handles. This adds +0.7 points at 8B and +0.3 at 32B. Completing persistent multimodal memory with visual attachments and reusable image handles adds further +3.1 and +4.5, bringing the full harness to 47.1 and 52.5. The largest gains from this final step occur in visual search and deep research (+6.2/+3.5), with additional gains in spatial reasoning (+2.8/+3.1). The results support the methods complementary mechanisms: interpretable tool observations, followed by retained multimodal artifacts that can be revisited and composed across turns.

sections.title: 3.5 FAILURE ANALYSIS
sections.content: We use Kimi K3 to critique 9,893 failed Qwen3-VL-8B trajectories across 22 benchmarks. Given the question, answer, images, trajectory, and toolbox, the critic assesses each tool call and identifies

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 4: Failure diagnosis and harness specialization with Qwen3-VL-8B. We critique failure trajectories using Kimi K3. (a) Distribution of failure causes across four domains. (b) Proposed remedies: grouped into creating task-specific tools (AC), updating harness text (Y), and no proposed remedy (Z). (c) Four datasets selected for contrasting remedy profiles: (orange) dominates ERQA and RealWorldQA, while AC (blue) dominates SparBench and FREAK-VQA. (d) Gains from harness search and tool generation over the unoptimized harness. Harness search is more effective on datasets dominated by text-level changes, while tool generation yields larger gains when task-specific tools are preferred. the trajectorys primary failure cause and proposes fix. Its labels agree with human annotations on 92% of 100 sampled failures. The protocol, coverage, and taxonomy are detailed in Appendix E.1. Surprisingly, we find that failure patterns differ across domains (Fig. 4a). Despite substantial overall gains, grounded perception remains challenging in crowded images with more than 25 objects, where missed or merged instances limit exhaustive detection. Such perception errors account for the dominant incorrect tool output category (75% of failures in this domain). Failures in visual search and deep research most often involve an omitted tool call (49%), while failures in spatial reasoning and in general VQA and hallucination involve both omitted tool calls and reasoning errors, consistent with our hypothesis that the model has limited proficiency in spatial reasoning and tool use. Failures involving unusable or ignored correct tool outputs are uncommon (38% across domains), suggesting that the capability layer generally presents retrieved evidence in usable form. Failure causes alone do not determine how to specialize the harness: an omitted call may require clearer instructions or new composition of tools. We therefore combine the cause and proposed fix into remedy channels (Fig. 4b). Constructing new task-specific tools can make evidence interpretation explicit (A), enforce systematic verification, filtering of tool results (B), or supply missing tool composition (C). In contrast, harness text changes (Y)edits to the system prompt, tool descriptions, and output messagesguide the model to call existing tools when needed and use their results appropriately. The remaining channel (Z) covers cases without proposed remedy. These diagnostic recommendations guide optimization rather than predict recoverable accuracy, since the critique covers only failed trajectories. Exact mapping rules and per-dataset shares are in Appendix E.2.

sections.title: 3.6 HARNESS OPTIMIZATION
sections.content: When adapting OpenVLHarness to custom domain, users can use failures on their own data to identify which parts of the harness need refinement. We provide two coding-agent-driven workflows for specializing the general-purpose harness without updating model weights. Harness search edits system prompts, tool descriptions, and evidence-rendering templates, selecting candidates through repeated evaluation. Tool generation implements and refines task-specific tools by composing existing capabilities (algorithms in Appendix E.3). To compare them, we select four datasets with contrasting remedy profiles (Fig. 4c): harness text changes (Y) dominate ERQA (71%) and RealWorldQA (56%), whereas task-specific tools (A+B+C) dominate SparBench (75%) and FREAK-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: VQA (62%). We run both workflows on all four datasets with Qwen3-VL-8B, testing whether their relative benefits align with these profiles. The results follow this distinction (Fig. 4d). Harness search improves ERQA and RealWorldQA by +4.1 and +3.7 points, compared with +0.2 and +0.1 from tool generation. Conversely, tool generation improves SparBench and FREAK-VQA by +8.2 and +4.5, while harness search yields 0.5 and 1.0. The generated tools compute metric 3D relations on SparBench and make visibility decisions explicit on FREAK-VQA, matching the missing-composition and evidence-interpretation needs identified by the critique  (Table 24)  . These results suggest practical approach to adaptation on custom data: diagnose the prevailing failures, then use harness search to improve the use of existing capabilities or tool generation to add the task-specific operations the domain requires.

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Visual Tool-Use Baselines. Early visual tool-use work treats the problem as program synthesis, compiling question into sequential plan that invokes vision tools in pipeline to produce an answer (Surıs et al., 2023; Gupta & Kembhavi, 2023; Kamali & Kordjamshidi, 2026; Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023b; Gao et al., 2023; Castrejon et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2024; Menon et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; You et al., 2023); because these plans are fixed in place, they cannot be adjusted based on tool execution results. later line adopts multi-turn frameworks that interleave reasoning with visual feedback, but depends on brittle, taskspecific framework designs that require extensive training to work (Ma et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026a; Su et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2026), and many domain-specific visual tool-use frameworks fall into the same category (Chen et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025a; Narayan et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d). Closest to our setting, Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) and OctoTools (Lu et al., 2025) are training-free tool-use frameworks built around manually designed tool interfaces and execution strategies. In contrast, we focus on making the harness itself more adaptable, so its evidence processing and tool composition can be specialized as tools, MLLMs, and target tasks evolve. Working Memory for Tool-Using Agents. Language agents maintain intermediate information to support reasoning and action across multiple steps. Context management approaches further separate compact model-visible state from more detailed external information, enabling the agent to selectively recover relevant content when needed (Packer et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024). Tool-using agents have also introduced explicit mechanisms for passing intermediate results across actions. ReWOO (Xu et al., 2023) represents tool evidence through referenceable variables, while CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024a) maintains intermediate results as variables in an executable interpreter. HuggingGPT (Shen et al., 2023) and LLMCompiler (Kim et al., 2024) go further in using symbolic references to intermediate tool outputs that are resolved when executing dependent downstream calls. Building on these ideas, OpenVLHarness extends them to the multimodal setting, maintaining unified registry of typed artifacts spanning images, structured data, and web evidence. It exposes compact model-facing handles while preserving the underlying artifacts for later inspection, composition, and reuse through modality-appropriate downstream tools.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented OpenVLHarness, general harness for real-world visual agentic tool use built around capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, enabling the orchestrator to invoke heterogeneous tools and inspect their outputs. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding artifacts for reuse across turns, including computation over stored data through Python Coding Agent. Together, these mechanisms support reasoning that acquires and composes multimodal evidence. Evaluation across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones demonstrates broad gains, while component ablations show the incremental benefits of the capability layer and multimodal memory. Harness search and tool generation further specialize the system on selected domains without updating the underlying MLLM weights. We release the harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and optimization workflows to support further work on multimodal tool-use agents.

sections.content: A TOOL-USE BEHAVIOR Table 1 reports the accuracy of OpenVLHarness. This section characterizes the behavior that produces it: how frequently the agent invokes tool, which capabilities it invokes, and how those invocations relate to accuracy relative to the same model without tools. The analysis covers five base models Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra, the GPT-6 models at medium reasoning effort and reads every rollout of the OpenVLHarness runs behind Tables 1 and 7, approximately 123,000 rollouts containing 224,000 tool calls. All counts are exact rather than sampled. question is engaged if the agent emitted at least one tool call on it, regardless of whether the call succeeded. Measurement protocol. Section A.3 compares OpenVLHarness against the Base columns of Tables 1 and 7 on per-question basis: both arms answer the same questions and are scored with the same dataset metric, and differences are averaged over paired rows. This design supports statements about individual capabilities, since the rows on which given tool was invoked can be isolated and both arms evaluated on that subset. The resulting quantities are correlational rather than causal: the agent selects the rows on which it invokes tool, and the remaining capabilities are available on those rows as well. Each per-tool measurement is therefore reported alongside control, namely the same paired difference computed on the rows that did not invoke the tool. capability whose two values coincide is not, on its own, responsible for the observed gain. The control is complement set, so its composition depends on how often the capability is invoked: for capability used on small fraction of questions the control approximates the models overall gain, whereas for one used on the majority of questions the control is small and atypical remainder. A.1 TOOL-CALL VOLUME AND ENGAGEMENT Two quantities characterize how heavily model uses the tools, and they vary independently: the number of calls question costs, and the fraction of questions answered with no call. Table 4 reports them per model, and Figure 5 resolves them by domain. Figure 5: Tool-call volume and engagement by domain. (a) Tool calls per question, averaged over all questions in the domain. (b) Fraction of questions answered with no tool call. Engagement varies with model scale within family and not across families, and call volume does not order the models by accuracy. Volume and engagement. Engagement varies with model scale within family but not across families. The smaller models leave substantial fraction of questions untouched (Qwen3-VL-8B 28.9%, GPT-6 Luna 25.3%), whereas the larger models rarely do (6.2%, 4.8% and 2.6%). Call volume does not order the models by accuracy: GPT-6 Luna issues the fewest calls per question of the five and attains higher accuracy than either Qwen model in Table 1. By domain, grounded perception engages all five models on nearly every question, while spatial reasoning and general VQA and hallucination account for most of the unengaged questions in the smaller models.

Calls per net gain divides the total number of tool calls issued on these questions by the net number of questions whose outcome changed. Aggregate effect. All five models improve under OpenVLHarness, by +6.2 (GPT-6 Astra) to +10.1 (Qwen3-VL-8B) points. The net figure is the balance of two considerably larger flows: between 2,336 and 4,649 questions per model are corrected, while between 700 and 2,146 are degraded. Normalizing by the tool calls spent, the cost of net corrected question ranges from 11.7 calls (GPT-6 Luna) to 28.1 calls (Qwen3-VL-32B), the latter combining the highest call volume with one of the smaller gains. Null control. On questions where the agent issued no tool call, OpenVLHarness reduces to the base model with longer system prompt, so the expected paired difference is zero. The measured values are 0.2 (GPT-6 Sol), 0.5 (GPT-6 Luna), 1.6 (Qwen3-VL-32B) and 1.8 (Qwen3-VL8B) points, and +1.8 for GPT-6 Astra, which leaves only 2.6% of questions without call, so its value rests on 614 questions. The proximity to zero supports the interpretation of the remaining differences as effects of tool use rather than of the prompt or the evaluation protocol, and the two larger negative values, both from the Qwen3-VL models, indicate small cost to carrying the tool interface when it is not used. Per-capability effects. Figure 8 reports, for each capability and model, the paired difference on the questions that invoked it. Table 6 gives the underlying counts, the share of questions each capability was invoked on, the accuracies of both arms, and the control, that is the same difference on the questions that did not invoke the capability. The two retrieval capabilities exhibit the largest separation from their controls in every model: rows invoking Image Search improve by 18.9 to 27.1 points, while the corresponding control values lie between 0.6 and +6.6. Visual Grounding is the dominant factor for the smaller models Qwen3-VL-8B improves by 14.3 points on rows that ground and declines by 20.1 points on rows that do not and flattens for the larger models, which invoke it on nearly all questions. Camera Trajectory is positive for all five models. Depth Estimation, OCR, Zoom-in and the Python Coding Agent are at or below their controls, apart from Zoom-in for GPT-6 Luna (+11.9 against +8.6) and GPT-6 Astra (+9.4 against +5.2), which is consistent with their being invoked on the questions model cannot resolve from the image alone rather than with their being ineffective in isolation.

The corresponding difference on the questions that did not invoke it, which serves as the control, is given in the last column of Table 6 together with the share of questions each capability was invoked on. A.4 CAPABILITY COMPOSITION Composition across capabilities. Rollouts frequently combine several capabilities rather than invoking one in isolation. Counting the number of distinct capabilities per rollout, among engaged rollouts 31.9% (Qwen3-VL-32B), 26.8% (GPT-6 Sol) and 26.0% (GPT-6 Astra) invoke two or more, against 20.7% and 11.6% for the smaller models, and the longest rollouts combine four or five. Combinations that cross capability families are rarer, 416% of engaged rollouts, and consist almost entirely of perception capability followed by the Python Coding Agent: ground or measure first, then compute over the resulting quantities. This is the pattern rewarded by the counting, grounding and spatial datasets, and it is not expressible in harness that exposes single capability.

sections.title: B ADDITIONAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: This section reports results with additional backbones (GPT-5, GPT-6 Sol, and Kimi K3), gives details of the ablation in Table 3, compares OpenVLHarness with training-based harnesses, analyzes grounded perception across object counts, extends the visual search and deep research results to 11 information-seeking benchmarks, and tests whether additional reasoning can replace the harness. B.1 ADDITIONAL BACKBONES Table 7 evaluates OpenVLHarness with GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025b), with GPT-6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026), and with Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026), an open-weight mixture-of-experts model with native visual understanding, on the same 22 datasets as Table 1, using the same tools, memory, prompts, and scoring. With GPT-6 Sol, OpenVLHarness improves every one of the 22 benchmarks, raising the average from 52.7 to 64.3.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: B.2 ABLATION STUDY DETAILS The ablation in Table 3 isolates the contribution of each harness component by building strict superset ladder: every rung adds exactly one mechanism to the one below it, so the gap between adjacent rungs measures that mechanisms marginal value. Variants. The five rungs are: 1. Baseline (no tool). The backbone model prompted directly with the question image and no tool access, establishing the no-harness floor. 2. + Tool. The nine tools are available, but their payloads arrive as raw dumps, their schema is cut to minimal signature (name, argument names and types, one clause each), and nothing persists between turns: no environment updates, no image labels, no data bindings, no URL references. Tool-generated images are replaced by short stub. 3. + Capability layer. Adds the capability layer of Sec. 2.1: each tools raw payload is replaced by per-tool post-processor that condenses it into concise, model-readable summary (e.g. grounding boxes on 01000 grid, reranked search results with inline citations, depth/zoom captions), and the full tool schema is restored so the model is told when to reach for each tool and how to phrase its arguments. No memory is presentnothing is carried across turns. 4. + Textual memory. Adds every memory mechanism that is addressed by text handle: per-turn Environment Updates that re-advertise all live state, webpage url references that let the agent revisit URL, and out-of-context data bindings that the Python Coding Agent can read as typed variables. Tool-generated images are replaced by VLM-written text description (up to 160 tokens) conditioned on the original question. Image references remain absent: tool-produced images cannot be named, stored, or passed to later tool call. 5. OpenVLHarness (full). Adds multimodal image memory: every tool-produced image is labeled (tool generated image N), deduplicated by content, and kept addressable. The model selects which image to pass to each tool call by its identifier, enabling compositions such as grounding zoom OCR search. Implementation. All five variants share the same nine-tool toolset, backbone weights, and decoding configuration (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, repetition penalty 1.0, presence penalty 1.5, up to 12,800 generated tokens per turn, 15 tool-calling iterations, 168K-token context cap). They differ only in the ablation preset applied to the memory stack: configuration block that switches individual mechanisms (environment updates, image identifiers, per-tool post-processors, data bindings, URL references) on or off. Each preset is strict superset of the one below it, validated at initialization so typo fails the run rather than silently selecting the wrong baseline. Table 8 summarizes the knob settings for each variant.

sections.content: Reasoners learned zoom-in behavior pays off. Training model into one tool protocol thus helps in-distribution but transfers poorly, whereas training-free harness can cover all four domains with the same weights. The backbone as orchestrator. Absolute scores with OpenVLHarness on Qwen2.5-VL-7B are well below those on Qwen3-VL  (Table 1)  . Because the harness relies on the backbone to plan tool calls and to follow output conventions, weaker orchestrator limits its benefit; on OdinW-13-All, for example, OpenVLHarness reaches only 7.80 AP with Qwen2.5-VL-7B versus 50.40 with Qwen3VL-8B. The harness therefore benefits directly from stronger backbones, with no retraining when new backbone is adopted. B.4 GROUNDED PERCEPTION ACROSS OBJECT COUNTS Most counting and grounding benchmarks rarely test models at high object counts, which can make headline scores misleading. To make this concrete, we bin every sample of widely used counting and grounding datasets by its number of target objects (Figures 9 and 10). For counting, TallyQA (Acharya et al., 2019), CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023), and PixmoCount place essentially all samples at ten or fewer objects; only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contribute meaningful mass above 50 objects. Grounding is even more skewed: referring-expression datasets such as RefCOCO/+/g (Kazemzadeh et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2016), Ref-L4 (Chen et al., 2024a), and GroundingME (Li et al., 2025a) ground exactly one target per sample, and detection-style benchmarks such as OdinW-13 and LVIS are dominated by single object per image (97% and 86% of samples in the 01 bucket). Dense, many-object grounding appears only in the FSCD variants. This is why our suite includes FSC-147, FSCD-147, and FSCD-LVIS, and why we break their results down by object count below. Figure 9: Object-count distribution across counting benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Widely used benchmarks such as TallyQA, CountBenchQA, and PixmoCount are dominated by low counts: nearly all of their samples contain ten or fewer objects (and majority of TallyQA fall in the 01 bucket), capping at 1015. Only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contain substantial mass in the high-count regime (> 50 objects), reaching into the hundreds or thousands. This skew means accuracy on standard counting benchmarks largely reflects performance on small object counts and reveals little about high-count visual measurement.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 10: Object-count distribution across grounding benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Referring-expression benchmarks such as RefCOCO/+/g and Ref-L4/GroundingME ground single target per sample (100% in the 01 bucket, max = 1), and even detection-style sets like OdinW-13 (97%) and LVIS (86%) are overwhelmingly concentrated at one object per image. Only the FSCD variants exercise dense, many-object grounding. As with counting, this distribution implies that progress on common grounding benchmarks is measured almost entirely in the singleor few-object regime.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Results by object count. Table 10 breaks down FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS by the number of ground-truth objects, using the bins defined above. On FSC-147, OpenVLHarness improves exactmatch accuracy in every bucket, with the largest gains between 11 and 50 objects (e.g., 5.0 32.9 at 8B for 2150), where the base models accuracy collapses. On FSCD-LVIS, where every image has at least 21 instances, the base models recover almost none of the instances (F1 12.5), whereas OpenVLHarness reaches F1 above 56 up to 100 instances and around 41 beyond. Accuracy nevertheless falls steeply with count for every configuration: above 100 objects exact counting remains essentially unsolved, confirming that the high-count regime is where the most headroom lies.

B.6 REASONING-EFFORT STUDY: SETUP AND FULL RESULTS OpenVLHarness answers question over several model calls, and each call carries tool outputs and memory, so it spends more model tokens per question than prompting the base model directly. This raises the question of whether the harness helps simply by spending more compute: reasoning model given larger token budget might recover the gain by reasoning for longer. GPT-6 Luna exposes reasoning-effort setting, which lets us test this directly by raising the effort of every method, including OpenVLHarness. Section 3.3 and Figure 1c summarize the results. Table 13 reports domain averages and costs, Table 14 the tokens per question behind the costs, Table 15 how often Codex executes code, and Table 16 the per-benchmark scores. Setup. We run Base, Codex, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness with GPT-6 Luna at five reasoning-effort settings (low, medium, high, xhigh, and max) on the full evaluation splits of all 22 benchmarks of Table 1, that is, 26,229 questions per setting and 524,580 in total. Each method keeps its configuration from Table 1 and Appendix G.1, and the medium-effort setting is the configuration reported in Table 1. Apart from the effort, only two settings change. First, Base, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness may produce up to 16,000 output tokens per model call, raised to 64,000 at max effort so that reasoning is not truncated; Codex uses its own default limit. Second, GPT-6 Luna accepts max effort only through the Responses API, so Base switches to that API at max effort; OpenVLHarness and Codex use it at every setting, and the Chat Completions requests of Visual Sketchpad are translated to it at every setting. The Python Coding Agent of OpenVLHarness uses the same reasoning effort as the orchestrator. Codex is the Codex CLI agent (OpenAI, 2025a, see Appendix G.1): every question runs in fresh session with the image attached and web search disabled to prevent the model from searching the web for the benchmarks gold answer, and modelwritten code executes in read-only sandbox enforced with Landlock and seccomp. All settings were run on the Flex service tier. Cost is the GPT-6 Luna API bill for model tokens: uncached input, cache reads and writes, and output, including hidden reasoning tokens. We price all settings at Standard-tier rates; the Flex tier halves every price and leaves cost ratios unchanged. Costs exclude tool execution (e.g., SAM 3, OCR, and search APIs) and judging, and are averaged over the 22 benchmarks in the same way as the scores. Scoring follows Table 1; on the search benchmarks, every setting is scored with the GPT-4o judge used in that table. question whose requests fail on every retry counts as incorrect; this occurred for 134 of the 524,580 questions (marked in Table 16). OpenVLHarness at medium effort (56.52 at $0.92 per 1,000 questions) exceeds every setting of every other method by at least 7.68 points; the strongest of those settings is Visual Sketchpad at max effort (48.84 at $5.15). Returns per unit of cost diminish for Base: moving from xhigh to max effort multiplies its cost by 2.7 and raises its average by 0.72 points. On FSC-147, no other setting exceeds 38.34, against 40.59 for OpenVLHarness at low effort; on the six search benchmarks, OpenVLHarness at max effort exceeds the best other setting by 3.0 to 19.6 points, and OpenVLHarness at low effort already exceeds it on 4 of them. Token usage. Most input tokens of OpenVLHarness, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad are cache reads and writes of the context carried across their model calls, whereas Base sends single prompt. For Base, raising the effort leaves the input unchanged at about 1,800 tokens per question and mainly increases reasoning tokens, from 301 to 5,852 per question between low and max effort. For the three harnesses, the input also grows between low and max effort: from about 8,000 to 11,800 tokens per question for Codex, from 20,800 to 24,100 for Visual Sketchpad, and from 14,500 to 24,600 for OpenVLHarness.

Capabilities and backends. Following the generalized capability abstraction of Section 2.1, each capability exposes fixed interface to the agent: typed arguments in, and natural-language message plus memory artifacts out. The expert model or service behind the interface is configurable backend, and switching it changes neither the agents prompt, the tool schema, nor the memory interface. Table 18 lists the capabilities and their backends; all experiments in this paper use the default backend of each capability, shown in bold.

C.1 SEARCH TOOLS By default, all three search tools route queries through the Serper API1; Text Search and Image Search can instead be served by Gemini (Comanici et al., 2025) with Google Search grounding, costlier but stronger route. The search tools post-process the raw payload with Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct model as the VLM summarizer. The summarizer runs at decoding temperature 0 with 4096-token output cap, and each call retrieves the top 10 raw results before reranking and summarization. Text Search. Search the web with intelligent query routing and VLM summarization. Given text query, the tool automatically classifies the query intent and routes it to the most appropriate Serper endpoint, which has general web, news, academic papers, images, maps, local places, shopping, or patents types, and returns coherent summary of the top-10 raw results with inline citations [1], [2], ... followed by citations block of source titles and URLs. This format supports multiround search: the agent can read the summary for quick understanding and then visit specific cited URLs through Webpage Visit. The summarizer prompt is shown below. sections.content: Please process the following webpage content and user goal to extract relevant information: Webpage Content: {webpage content} User Goal: {goal} Task Guidelines 1. Content scanning for rationale: locate the specific sections directly related to the users goal. 2. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: C.2 PERCEPTION TOOLS Zoom-in. Crop region of an image given normalized bounding box on the [0, 1000] scale plus padding, and return the cropped image. Used for closer visual inspection after the agent has already localized region of interest. Visual Grounding. Locate and highlight regions of an image that match text query, backed by SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025) by default or by Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024). It returns an annotated image with matched regions highlighted and numbered, along with bounding boxes (and segmentation masks when the backend provides them). OCR. Extract readable text from an image, backed by PaddleOCR-VL (PaddlePaddle Team, 2025) by default or by DeepSeek-OCR (Wei et al., 2025a). Returns the transcribed text as single string. Used when the task is about words, numbers, or printed labels in the image; not for general object localization or segmentation. Depth Estimation. Estimate per-pixel depth map for an input image, backed by Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) or VGGT (Wang et al., 2025b). Returns depth image (closer surfaces brighter, farther darker). Used when the task requires reasoning about relative distance, foreground background separation, or 3D scene structure cues that flat 2D crops cannot resolve. Camera Trajectory. Given an ordered sequence of at least two images of the same scene, estimate each cameras pose relative to the first image using Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) or VGGT (Wang et al., 2025b), and translate the result into form the model can reason over directly. Rather than returning raw geometry alone, the tool reports, for every image, plain-language summary of translation and rotation with respect to the reference frame (e.g. salient direction: backward (-5.43); detailed: left (-0.20), down (+0.28), backward (-5.43)), the accompanying scalars (cameracenter offset, forward direction, yaw, pitch), an explicit statement of the coordinate convention (+X right, +Y down, +Z forward, with positive yaw turning right), and birds-eye-view rendering of the camera positions on the reference frames XZ plane. Per-image intrinsics and world-tocamera extrinsics are returned as well for downstream computation. Translations below one meter and rotations below ten degrees are reported as non-salient. Used when question depends on how the viewpoint moved or rotated across frames, or on multi-view scene structure that no single image conveys; the estimate is metric only up to the models calibration and requires sufficient scene overlap between the reference image and the other views. C.3 PYTHON CODING AGENT Python Coding Agent. Run Python over the agents local computation state and the outputs of previously called tools (bounding boxes, OCR strings, segmentation masks, and so on), returning both standard output and the resulting local variables. The agent describes computation goal in plain language, and by default single-shot code-generation session of the same backbone model as the orchestrator writes the snippet using prior tool outputs as named variables before it is executed; the same interface can instead be backed by full coding agent that inspects and revises its own code before returning. Used for aggregating numbers extracted by OCR, filtering detected regions by bounding-box area, or any cross-tool numerical reasoning the agent cannot complete in its own response. C.4 MULTIMODAL MEMORY ARTIFACTS Table 19 summarizes how each tools output is retained in the explicit multimodal memory of Section 2.2 and the handle by which the agent re-addresses it on later turns. Open-source backbones. All Qwen models (Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen Team, 2025a) and Qwen3VL (Qwen Team, 2025b)) use the public Hugging Face weights, served in bf16 with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with native tool calling. We sample at temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, repetition penalty 1.0, and presence penalty 1.5, with up to 12,800 generated tokens per turn. The agent runs for at most fifteen tool-calling iterations per query, and its context is capped at 168K tokens; when trajectory approaches the cap, older turns are compacted while the latest Environment Update and the most recent turn are kept verbatim. Proprietary backbones. We call GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025b), GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026) through the OpenAI API with native function calling, providerdefault sampling, and up to 16,000 output tokens per turn. GPT-5 uses the pinned snapshot gpt-5-2025-08-07, and the three GPT-6 models (gpt-6-luna, gpt-6-sol, and gpt-6-astra) use medium reasoning effort. All four use the same tools, multimodal memory, system prompt, and iteration cap as the open-source backbones. Tool backends. Four tools call language model internally: Text Search and Image Search use it to rerank and summarize the retrieved results, Webpage Visit uses it to extract goal-relevant content from fetched page, and the Python Coding Agent uses it to write code for the agents objective. The three search-related tools use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with greedy decoding, independent of the agent backbone. The Python Coding Agent instead routes to fresh context of the same backbone model as the orchestrator, so that the code generators capability scales with the backbone. Every capability uses its default backend  (Table 18)  . Perception tools are backed by SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025) (Visual Grounding), PaddleOCR-VL (PaddlePaddle Team, 2025) (OCR), and Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) or VGGT (Wang et al., 2025b) (Depth Estimation and Camera Trajectory), each served locally; search tools query the Serper API. Judges. We use GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) with the Vision-DeepResearch judge prompt (Appendix D.2) for the visual search and deep research benchmarks, and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct for the remaining LLM-judged benchmarks; both judges decode greedily. On the counting benchmarks the judge only extracts the final integer from free-form responses, and correctness is decided by exact match. Grounding benchmarks need no judge and are scored with COCO-style box AP.

D.1 GROUNDED PERCEPTION FSC-147. class-agnostic counting benchmark (Ranjan et al., 2021) covering 147 categories with point annotation for every object. Scenes are dense (median 27 objects, up to 2,092). We evaluate on the 1,286-image val split and ask How many category are there in the image?. Unlike the original few-shot protocol, we do not provide exemplar boxes, so the task is zero-shot.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: CountQA. benchmark (Tamarapalli et al., 2025) of real-world counting questions designed to stress MLLMs with cluttered, occluded, and densely packed scenes. We use all 1,528 questions of the test split. OdinW-13-All. Built from the thirteen detection datasets of Object Detection in the Wild (OdinW13) (Li et al., 2022), spanning aerial and underwater imagery, egocentric hands, thermal images, vehicles, and everyday objects. Unlike the common protocol of querying one category at time, each image is posed as single query that lists every category of its source dataset (for example, all 20 PascalVOC classes), hence the suffix -All, and the model must return box with category label for every instance of every listed category. missed or mislabeled category therefore costs AP within the same response, and our numbers are not directly comparable to results obtained with one query per category. We use the 4,938 val images and report AP averaged over the thirteen datasets. FSCD-147 and FSCD-LVIS. The few-shot counting-and-detection benchmarks of Nguyen et al. (2022), which annotate box for every instance: FSCD-147 re-annotates FSC-147, and FSCD-LVIS draws dense scenes (21401 instances) from LVIS (Gupta et al., 2019). We use the val splits (1,286 and 1,181 images), query one category per image, and again withhold the exemplar boxes. LVIS (federated). In addition to the five benchmarks of Table 1, Appendix B.4 reports grounding on the LVIS val set (Gupta et al., 2019) (19,809 images, 1,203 categories) under its federated protocol, which queries both categories present in an image and verified-absent ones, so model must also learn to return an empty list. Counting metrics. Counting benchmarks are scored by exact-match accuracy between the predicted and ground-truth integers. rule-based parser extracts the integer (or number word) from the response; for long free-form responses, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct first extracts the final answer with the prompt below, and correctness is still decided by exact match. We additionally report mean absolute error and, for CountQA, relative accuracy within 5% and 10% of the ground truth (Appendix B.4). Grounding metrics. Grounding benchmarks are scored with COCO box AP averaged over IoU thresholds 0.50:0.95, computed with the official COCO evaluation code. Predicted boxes are parsed from the response (JSON, with lenient fallback for lists of four numbers) and converted from the 01000 grid to pixel coordinates. For OdinW-13-All, predicted labels are matched to the category names, AP is computed per source dataset, and the thirteen values are averaged. FSCD-147, FSCDLVIS, and LVIS are evaluated per queried category. No LLM judge is involved. Task prompts. All methods receive the same task prompts, shown below with category names as placeholders.

Answer extraction prompt (abridged) You are an AI assistant who will help me to extract the final answer from model response to visual question. You are provided with question, the ground truth answer, and the models response. Your task is to extract ONLY the final short answer from the response, matching the format of the ground truth (e.g. if the ground truth is number, extract number [. . . ]). Do NOT evaluate whether the answer is correct. Just extract it. If the response contains reasoning or explanation, ignore it and only return the final answer. [. . . three worked examples . . . ] Question: {question} Ground truth: {answer} Response: {response} swer: Extracted anD.2 VISUAL SEARCH AND DEEP RESEARCH FVQA. fact-based VQA dataset (Wu et al., 2025a) that pairs images with questions whose answers require commonsense or world-knowledge facts not directly observable in the image. Following Vision-DeepResearch (Huang et al., 2026), we evaluate on the official test split of 1,800 samples; all samples are search-required. MMSearch. multimodal search benchmark (Jiang et al., 2024) of 300 manually curated questions across 14 subfields, designed to assess large multimodal models as multimodal search engines. We evaluate on the End-to-End sub-task, which requires the agent to perform query understanding, retrieval, and answering in single pipeline. To align with other works for fair comparison, we only use the multimodal subset, which contains 171 samples. MMSearch-Plus. harder, provenance-aware extension (Tao et al., 2026) that emphasizes localized visual reasoning, verification under noisy or conflicting retrieval, and multi-step textimage search; each item provides 15 images and one or more valid answers. We use the full set of 311 samples for evaluation. BrowseComp-VL. The visionlanguage extension of BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025b) introduced by WebWatcher (Geng et al., 2026), with cross-modal information-seeking questions spanning entertainment, humanities, technology, natural science, and other domains. We use all 399 samples for evaluation. HLE-VL. The multimodal subset of Humanitys Last Exam (Phan et al., 2025), drawn from frontier-knowledge questions across mathematics, the natural sciences, and the humanities. We use all 330 samples for evaluation. RealX-Bench. Introduced by DeepEyesV2 (Hong et al., 2026a), it contains expert-verified instances that require integrating fine-grained visual perception, dynamic multi-hop web retrieval, and multi-step logical reasoning. This benchmark contains perception and search types, which makes it easy to attribute gains to visual versus search tools. We use all 194 samples for evaluation. Extended benchmarks. The following five benchmarks appear only in the extended search results (Appendix B.5, Table 12). They use the same judge and prompt as the six benchmarks above. MM-BrowseComp. Hand-crafted multimodal browsing questions (Li et al., 2025b) across several sub-tasks, where the answer-relevant content is hard to find. There are two versions of MMBrowseComp. We use the newest version, which has 243 multimodal tasks.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: VDR-Bench. The benchmark released alongside Vision-DeepResearch (Huang et al., 2026): longhorizon multimodal deep-research instances that interleave many reasoning turns, designed to evaluate sustained multi-step browsing under heavy real-world noise. We use its test-mini split of 500 samples. VisBrowse-Bench. benchmark of visual-native search instances (Zhang et al., 2026c) that require cross-validation of multimodal evidence via interleaved textimage retrieval and joint reasoning, including cases where the answer is not present in any text snippet. We use the full 169 samples for evaluation. InfoSeek. visual information-seeking benchmark (Chen et al., 2023) of fine-grained questions about entities depicted in images (e.g., species, models, landmarks). The official test split has no public answers, so we evaluate on the 2,000-sample test subset used by MMSearch-R1 (Wu et al., 2025a). EncyclopedicVQA. benchmark (Mensink et al., 2023) of questions about detailed properties of fine-grained categories. We draw random subset of 2,000 samples from the test split. 40 of its Google Landmarks v2 images are no longer publicly available, which leaves 1,960 samples for evaluation. No retrieval shortcut. Across all visual search and deep research benchmarks, we did not observe cases in which the search tools surface the gold answer verbatim from indexed pages. This reduces the likelihood that gains are driven by trivial retrieval of the gold answer. Judge prompt. To align with recent multimodal deep-research work (Huang et al., 2026), we adopt the same LLM judge and use GPT-4o as the judge model, applying the prompt below uniformly across all search-related benchmarks.

sections.title: LLM Judge Prompt
sections.content: You are an impartial judge evaluating whether deep research report contains the correct answer. [Question] {question} [Correct Answer] {correct answer} [Deep Research Report] {response} Task: Determine if the deep research report contains the correct answer anywhere in its content. Instructions: 1. Read through the entire research report carefully 2. Look for the correct answer anywhere in the report (it may be embedded in paragraphs, tables, or sections) 3. Check if the information in the report is consistent with the correct answer 4. The answer does NOT need to be in specific format or labelled as final answer 5. Provide your reasoning 6. Answer with yes if the report contains the correct answer, no if it doesnt or contradicts it Output format: correct: [yes/no] reasoning: [your explanation] Refusals on identity queries. Some of our evaluation benchmarks contain queries that reference real person, such as who is the person in this photograph, what is the affiliation of this researcher. Proprietary models are increasingly trained to decline such queries under their privacy and identification policies, even when the gold answer is public-figure fact already widely indexed on the open web. We observe this for the GPT models in our setting, which return refusal in place of an answer, which the judge counts as incorrect. Therefore, in some of the benchmarks, the GPT performance is affected to some extent.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: D.3 GENERAL VQA AND HALLUCINATION This domain tests whether tool use helps, or at least does not hurt, on everyday visual questions and on questions designed to provoke hallucination. RealWorldQA. Real-world photographs, many taken from vehicles, with multiple-choice questions about spatial layout and scene understanding (xAI, 2024); we use all 765 questions. SimpleVQA. factuality benchmark (Cheng et al., 2025) of short, knowledge-bound questions about images. We use all 2,025 questions and grade answers as correct or incorrect with an LLM judge. HallusionBench. Yes/no questions built from paired original and edited images and charts to expose language hallucination and visual illusion (Guan et al., 2024). Of the 1,129 questions in the released set, we evaluate the 951 that are grounded in an image. Free-form responses are first mapped to yes/no by an LLM extraction pass before scoring. The benchmark defines three accuracies: aAcc, the fraction of individual questions answered correctly; qAcc, the fraction of question groups for which every question is correct; and fAcc, the fraction of figures for which every associated question is correct. The latter two are deliberately strict, since model that answers from language priors tends to succeed on the original image and fail on its edited counterpart. We report the benchmarks Overall score, the unweighted mean of the three. FREAK-VQA and FREAK-MCQ. FREAK (Yin et al., 2026) asks about counter-commonsense images, where answering from priors rather than the pixels leads to hallucination, across detection, counting, attribute, position, and OCR questions. It comes in an open-ended format (799 questions, graded by an LLM judge) and four-option multiple-choice format (994 questions) that includes the correct answer is not listed. V*. Questions about small attributes and relative positions of objects in high-resolution images (Wu & Xie, 2024), where the relevant detail is easy to miss at the models input resolution; we use all 191 questions. D.4 SPATIAL REASONING The spatial reasoning benchmarks are multiple-choice, and several of them provide multiple views of scene, which exercises the harnesss handling of several input images. We follow the evaluation split used by the EASI leaderboard (Cai et al., 2025) and use its official implementation in the VLMEvalKit repository (Duan et al., 2024). MMSI-Bench. Multi-image spatial-intelligence questions (Yang et al., 2025b) spanning positional relations, attributes, motion, and multi-step reasoning across views; we use the 1,000 questions in the standard (non-circular) setting. ERQA. The embodied reasoning benchmark released with Gemini Robotics (Team et al., 2025), with 400 multiple-choice questions on spatial reasoning, trajectories, actions, and state estimation, some with several images. EmbSpatial-Bench. Spatial-relation questions posed from an egocentric viewpoint in embodied 3D scenes (Du et al., 2024); we use all 3,640 questions. SparBench. Spatial perception and reasoning tasks over single and multiple views (Zhang et al., 2026a). We use the tiny split: 20 tasks 50 questions = 1,000 questions. Tasks are scored by type. Eleven multiple-choice tasks (spatial relations, spatial imagination, position matching, cameramotion inference) are scored by option-match accuracy. Eight numeric tasks (depth and distance prediction, object-centric and object-to-object, singleand multi-view) are scored by mean relative accuracy (MRA), which averages the indicator that the relative error falls below threshold, sweeping the threshold from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, so partially accurate magnitude estimates receive partial credit. One task, view-change inference, uses the benchmarks own view-change metric. We

MindCube. Questions that require building mental model of scene from few partial views, covering among, around, and rotation settings (Wang et al., 2025c); we use the 1,040-question MindCube-Tiny split.

sections.title: E FAILURE ANALYSIS AND HARNESS OPTIMIZATION DETAILS
sections.content: This appendix describes how failure diagnosis guides specialization of OpenVLHarness on users data. We detail the critique protocol, the mapping from diagnoses to remedy channels, and the two workflows that modify harness text or add task-specific tools without updating model weights. We then provide examples of the resulting edits and tools. E.1 CRITIQUE PROTOCOL Failure selection and coverage. We use Kimi K3 to critique failures of the unoptimized OpenVLHarness with Qwen3-VL-8B, obtaining 9,893 completed critiques across 22 benchmarks. Failures follow each benchmarks judge verdict. For OdinW-13-All, FSCD-147, and FSCD-LVIS, which report box AP without per-image verdicts, we select images whose predicted boxes have F1 below 0.5 at IoU 0.5. Table 23 reports the completed coverage. Critic inputs and outputs. Each critique includes the question, reference and predicted answers, full trajectory, input and tool-generated images, and toolbox from the runs configuration. Tool descriptions and argument schemas are supplied with called tools marked, so the critic can assess omissions against the capabilities actually available. For each call, it labels information usefulness (yes, partial, or no) and correctness (correct, wrong, or unverifiable). It also returns one primary failure cause, proposed fix type and sketch, supporting transcript excerpts, and confidence, all in structured JSON record. Each critique uses approximately 3k prompt tokens and 0.72k completion tokens. Taxonomy. The critic separately identifies where the trajectory failed and what change could address it  (Table 22)  . build-tool fix requires new callable, including wrappers that verify, filter, or translate outputs and compositions of existing capabilities. text-only fix changes instructions for using existing tools. These labels are subsequently combined into remedy channels; they do not directly determine which workflow to use. Human agreement. Human annotators independently labeled 100 randomly sampled critiqued failures, with an average agreement of 92% with the critic. The abridged prompt below specifies the evidence requirements and fixed labels. Critic prompt (abridged) You are strict, evidence-driven critic of vision-language tool-using agent. You are shown ONE trajectory where the agent answered visual question wrongly, together with the correct answer and the catalog of tools the agent could call. [. . . ] The single question your critique must answer cleanly is: does fixing this family of failures require NEW TOOL CODE the agent can call, or only TEXT change? [. . . ] How to judge each tool call. For every tool the agent called, decide info useful (did the returned information bear on answering this question?) and info correct (was that information actually right, judged against the image content, the question, and the correct answer?). If grounding tool reports 3 boxes but the correct answer implies 5 objects, that output is wrong. If you cannot tell, say unverifiable; do not guess. tool output wrong, Root reasoning error, tool output unusable form, label or question issue. tool not called must name tool from the agents toolbox that would have supplied the missing evidence; if no listed tool could have, describe the missing capability in the fix sketch instead. [. . . ] tool output ignored, of tool not called,

sections.content: The needed evidence was never gathered, although tool in the agents toolbox could have supplied it. tool was called but returned wrong or missing information (missed or hallucinated boxes, bad crop, wrong transcription). tool returned correct information in form the model could not use (raw arrays, uninterpreted coordinates, an overload of detections). tool returned correct, plainly usable information that the model did not incorporate or contradicted. The evidence was adequate and used; the error is in reasoning, arithmetic, comparison, or answer format. The question is ambiguous or the reference answer looks wrong; the agents answer is defensible. new callable is needed: wrapper around base tool, combination of tools, or an output-translation layer. Only tool description or the agent prompt changes. Nothing above would plausibly help. Table 22: Critique taxonomy. Each failure receives one primary cause and one proposed fix type. Unusable and ignored outputs remain separate during critique and are combined for reporting in Fig. 4 and Table 23. Rules. Ground every claim in the transcript: quote the tool output or the agents text. Never assume tool was right just because the agent believed it. Do not propose memorizing answers or matching question wording; fix sketch must describe general capability or change. Set confidence low when the evidence is thin. Return ONLY JSON object. E.2 REMEDY CHANNELS AND PER-DATASET RESULTS Each failed trajectory receives two labels from the critic: root cause, describing where it failed, and fix type, indicating whether the proposed remedy requires new tool code, text change, or neither. We determine its remedy channel jointly from this pair, using the tool-call assessments where needed. For example, an omitted call paired with build-tool fix maps to tool composition (C), whereas the same cause paired with text-only fix maps to harness text (Y). The channels distinguish adding task-specific tools (A+B+C) from refining harness text (Y). New tools can make evidence interpretation explicit, refine outputs, or compose existing capabilities. Harness text comprises the system prompt, tool descriptions, and evidence-rendering templates; editing it guides when existing tools are called and how their results are used. We first assign cases with fix type none or question/reference-answer issue to Z, then map the remaining causefix pairs as follows: A: evidence interpretation tools. An ignored-output or reasoning-error cause paired with build-tool fix. We also include text-only fixes for ignored outputs, or for reasoning errors when at least one call returned correct, at least partially useful evidence. These tools turn available evidence into explicit task-level conclusions that the model can more readily use. B: output verification and refinement tools. wrongor unusable-output cause paired with build-tool fix, motivating systematic verification, filtering, or translation. C: tool composition. An omitted-call cause paired with build-tool fix, motivating taskspecific callable that combines existing capabilities into the required operation. Y: harness text for tool-use guidance. The remaining causes paired with text-only fix. Z: no proposed remedy. Cases excluded above because no fix is proposed or the question/reference answer is problematic.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: The motivation for is that correct, useful evidence may still require interpretation before it supports an answer. reasoning error despite such evidence can therefore indicate difficulty interpreting or incorporating it, as can an ignored output. We include these cases even when the critic proposes text change, to test whether tool that makes the relevant conclusion explicit can address the difficulty. This motivates candidate remedy rather than establishing that interpretation caused every such failure. Table 23 reports the channel shares among critiqued failures. The final column illustrates why an omitted call alone does not identify the remedy: the critic proposes new tool code for 70% of such failures on SparBench, but only 11% on ERQA. The four datasets in Sec. 3.6 span contrasting profiles: accounts for 71% of ERQA and 56% of RealWorldQA failures, while A+B+C account for 75% of SparBench and 62% of FREAK-VQA failures. These shares guide the choice of workflow; they do not predict accuracy gains. Critiques of failures alone cannot establish whether an edit harms previously correct answers or whether the orchestrator will use generated tool. Root cause (%) Remedy channel (%)

The RealWorldQA example below combines edits from three search rounds: five system-prompt additions and one addition to the Visual Grounding output template. They guide the orchestrator to inspect small road-scene details, verify counts, and match its visual conclusion to the answer options. The output-template edit illustrates how evidence rendering supports adaptation: it prompts verification of grounded candidates before they are used as counts or relation evidence. Edits in top-scoring RealWorldQA harness (additions only) System prompt, when to use visual tools. For road-scene details such as traffic lights, traffic signs, arrows, lane markings, and whether driver must stop, use visual tools before answering unless the relevant mark or signal is unmistakably large and clear. Before answering that such detail is absent, not visible, or has particular color/direction, ground the likely object or region and inspect the original pixels with zoom if the region is small or distant. System prompt, using tool results. For count questions with numeric options, compare the filtered candidate count with the option values. If the count is outside the listed values or directly adjacent to listed value, do one missed-object check using broader/simple phrase or one targeted zoom of the most uncertain region, then choose the listed option best supported by all evidence. For counts of printed letters, digits, or symbols, use OCR or text-focused zoom when available before deciding the count. Unless the question explicitly says standalone, count occurrences inside longer strings as well as isolated characters. System prompt, final answer. For multiple-choice questions, before writing <answer>, explicitly bind your visual conclusion to the option table. The option letter and option text you output must match each other and match the conclusion in your thinking; if your conclusion is not one of the options, re-check the evidence instead of choosing nearby option. If the listed options do not include none/unknown/cannot-determine choice, never use an unlisted absence answer such as none of the above, not visible, or cannot tell. If your draft conclusion is that the needed cue is absent, do one targeted visual check when tool can resolve it, then answer with the listed option best supported by the evidence. Visual Grounding output template (appended after the list of boxes). Treat these as candidate regions, not verified final count. Before answering count, presence, or relation questions, compare each candidate with the original image and remove duplicates, mirror/reflection copies, partial regions, offtarget detections, and objects that fail the questions location or context constraint.
