sections.content: This section shows seventeen complete OpenVLHarness trajectories, ordered as the datasets appear in Table 1: grounded perception (Examples 13), visual search and deep research (Examples 49), general VQA and hallucination (Examples 1012) and spatial reasoning (Examples 1317). Eleven come from GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, taken from the runs behind Table 1; six come from OpenVLHarness runs of Qwen3-VL-32B. Each example starts on new page under dark title bar and ends with an End of Example rule, and every step header names its example. Each example is laid out the same way: Overview and step notes. Each example opens with green overview box that explains in plain words what the task asks, why it is hard without tools, and how the agent solves it. For the proprietary GPT-6 models, each step then opens with short green What happens note that says what the call does and why it matters. We add these notes only for proprietary models, whose reasoning traces we cannot access: the API returns the tool calls and any visible text, but not the models reasoning, and GPT-6 often calls tool without writing any text at all. The open Qwen3-VL models expose their reasoning, which they write in <thinking> tags before each call and which we show verbatim, so their examples have no step notes. The overviews and notes are our descriptions, written to guide the reader; everything else in the trajectory is verbatim. Inputs, question and results. The input images and the question exactly as sent to the model, then table comparing the answer with and without the harness against the ground truth. For grounded perception examples, the table also shows what SAM 3, the model behind Visual Grounding, returns when queried alone, where the trajectory makes that measurable. For some Qwen3-VL examples no run of the same model without tools is available, and the table says so. Without tools. The same models full response to the same question with no tools, where such run exists. Full trajectory with OpenVLHarness. Every tool call in order. Each step shows the tool, colour-coded by family (perception, search, computation); the complete arguments the model sent; the text the model wrote alongside the call, when there is any; the tools output, including the complete code the coding agent wrote and its execution output; and every image the tool returned, which the model sees in its next turn. For grounding examples, whose final answer is list of coordinates, we add panel drawing the final boxes on the input image, marked as ours. Harness messages. On cream background : the environment updates through which the multimodal memory tells the model what it currently holds (Appendix C.4), including the data bindings that pass tool results to the coding agent. What to notice. closing note on how the harness contributed. All model text, arguments and tool outputs are verbatim, generated directly from the trajectory files. To keep each example readable we shorten in five ways, and every cut is marked in red where it happens. Search results show their first two entries, with the number omitted. Coding-agent execution outputs longer than 70 lines keep their first 25 and last 10 lines; the code itself is always complete. coding-agent run that failed with an error shows the error but not its code. Other tool outputs longer than 1,500 characters are cut, with the remaining length stated; one such output in Example 11 is webpage summary that loops, repeating the same sentences for over 128,000 characters. After the first environment update, which is shown in full, each update is summarized as the memory entries it adds, with any new data bindings kept verbatim. We also show escaped newlines inside JSON strings as line breaks, and emoji in search results as [emoji] or [flag]. In Example 5 the question and the models reasoning are in Chinese; the overview translates the question. The system prompt is given in Appendix C.5. The examples were chosen by hand to illustrate how the harness composes tools, and are not random sample. Not every one is clean win, and the overviews say so where it matters: in Example 3 the no-tool answer fails on coordinate format; in Example 4 the perception step does not contribute; and in Examples 17, 14 and 9 the final answer is correct but only partly supported by the trajectorys evidence.

sections.content: Example 1 Dataset: FSC-147 Model: GPT-6 Sol Overview (our summary) Task. Count the pills in photograph of about 140 pills of many colours and two shapes, oblong capsules and small round tablets, scattered on dark surface. Why it is hard. There are too many to count reliably by eye, and single detector query does not reliably find both shapes. How the agent solves it. It runs two grounding queries, one general and one for round pills, then asks the coding agent to merge the two sets of detections without counting any pill twice. The first merge fails silently; the agent notices the impossible result and rewrites the merge, which then finds the five pills the first query missed. sections.content: Example 17 Dataset: SparBench Model: Qwen3-VL-32B Overview (our summary) Task. Three photographs of an office corner are taken from nearby positions. red point marks window in the first photo and blue point marks cabinet in the third. Give the 3D distance between them in metres. Without tools the same model answers 1.7 m. How the agent approaches it. It chains four kinds of tool: camera trajectory to relate the views, depth in all three views, grounding to locate the window and the cabinet, and the coding agent to back-project both points into one frame and measure between them. Caveat. The pipeline is the right one, but its last step does not use the marked points. The generated code reads each box as position plus width and height, although the boxes are corner coordinates, and it takes the first cabinet box, an upper wall cabinet at the top edge of the photo, instead of the lower cabinet with the blue point. The answer, 1.20 against ground truth of 1.1 m, is therefore close partly by coincidence. INPUT IMAGES input image input image 2 input image 3 QUESTION (as sent to the model) Question: In meters, how far is the center of window (red point) from the center of cabinet (blue point)? numeric value is required for your response. Please answer the question using single word or phrase. Calculate or judge based on the 3D center points of these objects.

sections.content: We re-run every baseline ourselves on our benchmark suite using each methods official implementation  (Table 25)  . All baselines receive exactly the same question text as OpenVLHarness, including each datasets answer-format instruction (e.g., single integer, or JSON list of boxes on 0 1000 scale for grounding); the only addition is short answer-format instruction that Codex appends for Qwen3-VL backbones (Appendix G.1). Their predictions are scored with the same evaluation pipeline and judges. Boxes that baseline returns in different coordinate frame, such as pixel coordinates of the models resized input, are converted to our normalized format before scoring. Every baseline is evaluated on the full evaluation split. On Qwen3-VL, OctoTools and Visual Sketchpad follow the same three-run protocol as OpenVLHarness (Appendix H); runs with proprietary backbones and the training-based baselines are single runs. request that fails or times out counts as incorrect.

sections.title: OpenVLHarness Matched to baseline
sections.content: Nine tools  (Table 18)  Table 25: Configurations of the reproduced baselines. Search marks access to web-search tool. All baselines except Codex decode greedily; Codex uses its own request settings. G.1 TRAINING-FREE HARNESSES The training-free harnesses run on the same model endpoints as OpenVLHarness, so any difference reflects the harness rather than the model. OctoTools. OctoTools (Lu et al., 2025) is plannerexecutor framework in which planner analyzes the query and proposes the next step, an executor turns it into tool command, and verifier decides whether to stop. We use the official implementation and route every language-model role, including the planner, executor, verifier, and the Generalist Solution Generator tool, to the Qwen3VL backbone. We use its base toolset, the Generalist Solution Generator, with budget of ten steps and greedy decoding. Because OctoTools accepts single image per query, multi-image inputs are tiled into one composite with labeled panels (Image 1, Image 2, . . . ). The final answer is taken from its direct-output mode. Visual Sketchpad. Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) prompts the model to write Python that calls vision tools and draws on the image, in ReAct-style loop. We use the official implementation with the Qwen3-VL backbone as its single planning agent and its vision-task toolset: open-vocabulary detection with Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024), sliding-window detection, Set-of-Mark segmentation (Yang et al., 2023a), depth estimation with Depth Anything (Yang et al., 2024), zoom-in, and image overlay, all served with the original expert models. The agent may take up to ten replies with greedy decoding, receives multiple images as separate inputs, and ends with an ANSWER: line from which we read the prediction. For grounding tasks, it is instructed to convert its detectors boxes to our output format. Codex. Codex (OpenAI, 2025a) (v0.155.1) is OpenAIs general-purpose coding agent. We run it non-interactively (codex exec) in code mode, with fresh, ephemeral session for every question, the questions images attached as inputs, and its final agent message taken as the prediction. Web search, browser use, apps, plugins, image generation, and sub-agents are disabled, and modelwritten code runs in read-only sandbox. With GPT-6 Luna, Codex calls the OpenAI Responses API at medium reasoning effort and receives the question text unchanged. Codexs default sandbox cannot start shell processes on our evaluation host. For the GPT-6 Luna runs, we therefore enforce the same read-only policy with Linux Landlock and seccomp, under which model-written code executes (Table 15 reports how often); the Qwen3-VL runs used the default sandbox and could evaluate only simple expressions (Appendix B.7). With Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B, it calls the same vLLM endpoints as OpenVLHarness through small proxy that exposes Codexs code tool as standard function tool, which our vLLM server otherwise fails to stream, and each response is capped at 2,048 tokens. For the Qwen3-VL runs, Codex also appends short instruction to the question: answer directly, give the option letter for multiple-choice questions, and use the image as evidence. question whose request fails or exceeds the time limit counts as incorrect; the limit is 300 seconds with Qwen3-VL and 1,800 seconds with GPT-6 Luna. With Qwen3-VL, LLM-judged benchmarks, including the search benchmarks, are scored with the Qwen3-VL-8B judge; with GPT6 Luna, scoring follows Table 1, so the search benchmarks are scored with the GPT-4o judge.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: G.2 TRAINING-BASED HARNESSES For the training-based baselines, the tool-use behavior lives in the fine-tuned weights, so we evaluate each methods released checkpoint inside its authors inference loop rather than re-training it. We followed two-stage reproduction procedure. First, we executed each repositorys own reproduction workflowincluding its released environment, model checkpoint, prompt and image preprocessing, tool implementations, and agent loopuntil the baseline ran correctly on its documented benchmarks. Second, we added lightweight HTTP serving layer around that verified path. The serving layer standardizes request transport, process lifecycle, and input normalization, while the model-specific reasoning logic remains in the released implementation. Each service accepts question and one or more ordered images, returns final prediction and an agent trajectory, and keeps the model and tool processes resident across examples. All hosted baselines are evaluated through shared external harness. For each benchmark example, the harness invokes the datasets prompt builder, converts the resulting text and ordered images into common request, and records the returned prediction. The harness controls outer concurrency and, after inference, writes the prediction file expected by the benchmark evaluator and invokes the datasets native evaluate method using the same configured language-model judge where required. Crucially, scoring is performed entirely outside the baseline services: no service inspects ground truth, selects an evaluator, or computes accuracy. This separation ensures that all baselines are scored through single consistent protocol. We compare them against OpenVLHarness on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, the base model all three were fine-tuned from  (Table 9)  . AdaReasoner. AdaReasoner (Song et al., 2026) trains the model to adaptively compose tools. We use the AdaReasoner-7B checkpoint and the authors BaseToolInferencer, which exposes pointing (backed by Molmo (Deitke et al., 2025)), OCR, cropping, and drawing and path-planning tools through <tool call> blocks, for up to six rounds. AdaReasoner is the only baseline requiring two Conda environments: the model/vLLM stack and the GPU PaddleOCR tool workers have incompatible tested dependencies. The launcher starts tool controller and dedicated Point, OCR, and Crop workers alongside the model server. PixelReasoner. PixelReasoner (Wang et al., 2025a) is trained to reason in pixel space. We use the PixelReasoner-RL-v1 checkpoint and initialize the released Ray/vLLM engines, multimodal processor, and function-call prompt once at startup. The service retains the released tool parser and pixel-space operations (normalized cropping and frame selection). Inference proceeds at the granularity of model/tool rounds: ready requests are batched across vLLM engines, generated tool calls are executed, resulting crops or selected frames are appended to the conversation, and unfinished requests are requeued. The final answer is read from boxed{}. The documented image-resolution budgets (MIN PIXELS=401408, MAX PIXELS=4014080) are preserved as they affect how much visual information reaches the model. DeepEyesV2. DeepEyesV2 (Hong et al., 2026a) is trained for agentic multimodal reasoning with code execution. We use the released DeepEyesV2-7B checkpoint with the agent mode of the authors vendored VLMEvalKit VLLMAPIWrapper. single launcher supervises the text-search adapter, Python code service, one or more OpenAI-compatible vLLM model replicas, and the public inference API. The wrapper controls model calls, Python execution, retrieval turns, stopping rules, and answer extraction. All ordered input images are bound in the Python sandbox as image 1, image 2, . . . so that generated code can address every input. Fair-comparison controls. For defensible comparison, the following are held fixed or explicitly reported across all baselines: dataset version, split, and prompt builder; model checkpoint and quantization; image preprocessing and resolution limits; context window, per-call generation cap, temperature, and maximum agent/tool rounds; enabled tools and external search backend; concurrency and failure-retry policy; judge model, judge prompt, and judge retry count; and whether failures are scored as incorrect or retried.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: H RUN-TO-RUN VARIABILITY Agentic evaluation is stochastic: the backbone samples at non-zero temperature, the harness makes further model calls inside its tools, and live search results change over time. This section describes how we account for this variability and quantifies it for the Qwen3-VL results in the main paper. Protocol. Every Qwen3-VL number in the main paper, including the Base, OctoTools, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness columns of Table 1 and every entry of Table 3, is the mean of three independent runs. Each run uses different random seed, which controls both the backbones sampling and every stochastic component of the harness, such as the model calls made inside the Webpage Visit and Python Coding Agent tools. All other factors are held fixed across runs: the benchmark instances, prompts, tool backends, decoding parameters, iteration and context limits, and the scorers. Judges and answer extractors decode greedily, so the variation we measure comes from the agent rather than from scoring. We report all three runs of every configuration; no run is discarded or re-run, and request that fails after retries is scored as incorrect in the run where it occurs. Search tools query the live web and cannot be seeded, so for search benchmarks the variation also reflects changes in retrieved content between runs. Results with proprietary backbones (GPT-5, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra) are single runs because of API cost. Reported statistics. Tables 26 and 27 report, for each entry, the standard deviation of the score across the three runs. For averages over datasets, we first compute the average within each run and then take the standard deviation of these three averages; this is smaller than the per-dataset deviations because independent fluctuations partly cancel. With only three runs, each standard deviation is itself coarse estimate and should be read as indicating the scale of run-to-run variation rather than an exact value. Main results. Per-dataset standard deviations are small relative to the differences between methods  (Table 26)  . For OpenVLHarness, most are below 2 points; the largest occur on search benchmarks with live retrieval, such as MMSearch (171 questions, where one question is worth 0.58 points) and FVQA with Qwen3-VL-8B. OpenVLHarness varies somewhat more than Base, as expected for multi-turn trajectories in which an early difference in tool call can change the rest of the trajectory. The 22-dataset averages are very stable, with standard deviations of at most 0.35 points. The gain of OpenVLHarness over Base in this average (+11.2 at 8B and +12.6 at 32B) is therefore about 29 and 44 times the combined standard deviation of the two averages, so the improvement cannot be attributed to run-to-run variation. Ablation. The overall averages in Table 3 have standard deviations between 0.2 and 0.35 points for every variant and backbone  (Table 27)  . Adding tools, the capability layer, and multimodal memory each changes the overall average by several points, far beyond this variation. The textual-memory step (+0.7 at 8B and +0.3 at 32B) is comparable to run-to-run variation, which is consistent with our conclusion that text descriptions of images are weak substitute for retaining the images themselves. Single-run results. Proprietary backbones are evaluated once, so their per-dataset numbers carry run-to-run variation of the scale measured above. Their conclusions, however, rest on large differences: OpenVLHarness improves the 22-dataset average by +10.8 points with GPT-6 Luna, +11.6 with GPT-6 Sol, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra, more than twenty-five times the largest average-level standard deviation we observe with Qwen3-VL.

sections.title: I ADDITIONAL RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multimodal search agents. Our work targets multimodal search, where query is resolved by orchestrating reasoning, perception, and live web retrieval across many turns. growing collection of benchmarks frames this task: MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2024) couples multimodal query with curated search engine; MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026) adds provenance-aware verification; BrowseComp-VL (Geng et al., 2026) and MM-BrowseComp (Li et al., 2025b) raise cross-modal information-seeking difficulty; VisBrowse-Bench (Zhang et al., 2026c) targets visual-native search; and RealX-Bench (Hong et al., 2026a) couples fine-grained perception with multi-hop retrieval. Beyond pure search, the landscape extends to embodied tasks that integrate web information with physical action (Hong et al., 2025). Recent browsing agents tackle these benchmarks via hand-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: engineered tool inventories (Geng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025a; Narayan et al., 2025), supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning that teaches tool use, or memory learned over fixed inventory (Xiao et al., 2025; Hasegawa et al., 2025). Our contribution is orthogonal: rather than freeze the inventory, we generate it. Grounded perception. Class-agnostic counting was popularized by FSC-147 (Ranjan et al., 2021), which asks for the number of objects of an arbitrary category; specialized counters such as CounTR (Liu et al., 2022), LOCA (Djukic et al., 2023), and CountGD (Amini-Naieni et al., 2024) regress density maps or detections, and FSCD (Nguyen et al., 2022) extends the task to predicting box for every instance. Open-vocabulary detectors and segmenters, including GLIP (Li et al., 2022), Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024), and SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025), localize arbitrary text-specified categories, and MLLMs have begun to count by pointing (Deitke et al., 2025). Nevertheless, MLLMs remain unreliable once scenes contain more than handful of objects (Paiss et al., 2023; Tamarapalli et al., 2025). Tool-use systems such as ViperGPT (Surıs et al., 2023), VisProg (Gupta & Kembhavi, 2023), and Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) let language model call detectors and count their outputs programmatically. OpenVLHarness follows this direction but keeps grounding outputs as persistent evidence: boxes, masks, and scores are stored as typed bindings that the Python Coding Agent can filter, deduplicate, and aggregate across turns, instead of count that is read once from text. Spatial reasoning. Spatial reasoning benchmarks test models beyond static single-image relations. EmbSpatial-Bench (Du et al., 2024) and ERQA (Team et al., 2025) target spatial and embodied reasoning in simulated and real-world scenes; SparBench (Zhang et al., 2026a) covers diverse singleand multi-view spatial tasks; and MindCube (Wang et al., 2025c) and MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025b) emphasize reasoning across multiple or limited views. In parallel, VGGT (Wang et al., 2025b) and subsequent VGGT-style geometric foundation models (Hu et al., 2026) recover explicit scene geometry, including depth, camera pose, point maps, and tracks from visual observations. OpenVLHarness treats such geometric models as callable capabilities rather than requiring the MLLM itself to internalize 3D reconstruction, allowing their outputs to be composed with grounding and other persistent evidence during reasoning. Experience learning and harness optimization. Learning from past experience has long history in reinforcement learning, exemplified by Hindsight Experience Replay (Andrychowicz et al., 2017), which relabels failed rollouts as successes, STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022), which bootstraps reasoner on its own correct rationales, and ARMAP (Chen et al., 2025b), which learns reward model from an agents own trajectories to guide its planning. newer line treats memory as learning signal, distilling reusable knowledge from cross-sample working memory, though these methods often require additional training or model-weight updates (Packer et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2025a; Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025a; Ren et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026). third line instead optimizes prompts and harnesses without any model-weight updates, using LLMand coding-agent-driven optimizers that rewrite prompts, pipelines, and harness code from observed failures (Khattab et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Sharma, 2025), but to date this is done purely in the text-only prompt and harness domain.
